activities.anchor: M. A. K. Halliday's register theory decomposes
activities.caption: pair each dial with the linguistic reflex it selects
activities.name: risDialsMatch

config.prompt: The three dials of situation — pair each with the feature it selects:

pairs.left: field — what is being talked about

pairs.right: politeness, formality, the T–V pronoun choice
density and structure: writing nominalises, speech hesitates
outsider status, signalled faster than any grammar slip

config.why: One message, four keys: the professor email, the friend text, the workplace channel and the partner note were all grammatical — the dial, not the grammar, is what natives use to place each other.

activities.caption: file each feature by its direction of travel
activities.name: risMarkerBuckets

config.prompt: As formality rises, features climb, fall or track the relationship — file each:

items.label: "the implementation of the policy" instead of "when they put the plan in place"
nominalisation packing processes into analysable things
fillers and casual discourse markers: "like", "you know"
the T–V choice: tu/vous, du/Sie, tú/usted
office jargon as compression and membership badge: "let's circle back"

config.why: Density and nominalisation climb; contractions and fillers drop; hedging and pronoun choice encode social distance — and the register-switching drill (say it to a judge, a friend and a five-year-old) makes your own dial settings visible.

activities.anchor: Erman and Warren's corpus estimate puts it
activities.caption: bet on the chunk share of real discourse
activities.name: risChunkEstimate

config.prompt: What share of real spoken and written discourse is prefabricated chunks rather than novel combinations?
config.why: About half: natives sound fast because they assemble from ready-made blocks — which is why memorising high-frequency chunks beats generating word by word, and why idioms must be learned whole, with their social settings attached.
config.context: Deploy "kick the bucket" in a condolence message and you have an error no grammar checker would catch.

activities.caption: find the line the vocabulary-myth would love
activities.name: risIdiomSpot

config.prompt: One line of this summary is the vocabulary-myth speaking — click it:
lines: Idioms are frozen forms: "kick the bucket", never "kick the bucket violently, twice by John".
A large vocabulary is enough to work any idiom out from its words.
"Kick the bucket" is informal and faintly comic — a condolence-message hazard.
Word-for-word rendering yields nonsense: Dutch "it rains old women and pikesticks".
Idioms learned from shows and conversations arrive with frequency and social setting pre-installed.
config.correction: Frozen means the sense cannot be assembled from the parts — quasi-transparent ones are the most dangerous precisely because you think you follow them.
config.why: Chunk inventory, not word count, drives fluency — and idioms from lists arrive without the social settings that decide whether they fit.

activities.anchor: the native equivalent of a dad saying
activities.caption: run the slang decision in real time
activities.name: risSlangBranch

config.root: You are out with people your age in the target-language city. Someone drops a slang item you have heard exactly once, three months ago. You want to belong. What do you do with that item?

start.text: The item is current, in-group, and you are not sure of its edges. First decision:

choices.label: Deploy it immediately — belonging demands production
choices.feedback: Production is a status bet: misfired slang reads as trying too hard, and a misfire is remembered.

choices.label: Bank it for recognition, keep producing neutral choices
choices.feedback: Comprehension is risk-free and always useful — the asymmetry rule at work.

choices.label: Steer clear of slang altogether tonight
choices.feedback: Total avoidance has a cost too: it reads as distant or stiff.

bet.text: You used it. It landed oddly — a pause, a half-smile. What happened?

choices.label: You broke a context boundary you could not see
choices.feedback: Slang is context-bound: office, school and internet varieties barely overlap, and one item does not transfer across them.

check.text: When would producing it become the right call?

choices.label: Once you have heard speakers of your own age-and-context profile use it
choices.feedback: Exactly — the subscription rule: only current, in-the-wild input keeps an item working.

choices.label: Once a dictionary lists it
choices.feedback: Too slow: by the time a dictionary prints a term, its young users may have moved on.

distant.text: You stayed silent and formal all evening.

choices.label: Reconsider the middle path
choices.feedback: Recognise everything, produce selectively — the symmetric dilemma has a known exit.

lesson.text: Recognise everything, produce selectively — and only items you have heard from speakers of your own age-and-context profile.

config.why: The dilemma is symmetrical — wrong slang tries too hard, no slang reads distant — and recognition is risk-free while production is a bet; verlan (meuf from femme) and internet coinages turn over too fast for memorised lists.

activities.anchor: Beneath all three layers runs pragmatics
activities.caption: drag the divider — two softening sites for one face-threat
activities.name: risPoliteCompare

config.prompt: One face-threat, two softening sites — drag the divider:

before.label: English: soften with hedges and questions
before.text: "I was wondering whether..." is not a question about wondering — indirectness scales with social distance and power.

after.label: Japanese: build respect into the grammar
after.text: Whole grammatical systems of honorifics carry the face-work; requests wrap themselves in negatives and conditionals to preserve the other's option to refuse.

config.why: German directness reads as rude to a hedging culture and honest to itself — and pragmatic transfer is the C1 learner's most persistent residue: a grammatically perfect request imported from your first language's system can still strike locals as curt or obsequious.

activities.caption: pair each connective device with its example
activities.name: risCohesionMatch

config.prompt: The C1 essay's connective tissue — pair each mechanism with its example:

pairs.right: this, such, the latter — pointing back without repeating
the policy — the reform — the legislation

config.why: Weak: four standalone sentences about a factory closure, none pointing anywhere. Strong: one sentence — "The factory — closed suddenly, without consultation — took 400 jobs with it; for a town of 9,000, the closure was less an event than a change of identity" — carrying every device at once.

activities.anchor: The politeness layer becomes concrete when you compare
activities.caption: bet on what the refusal really said
activities.name: risRefusalPredict

config.q: A request to a Japanese counterpart draws the answer: "that would be a bit difficult." What has most likely arrived?
choices: A maybe — push gently and it will become a yes
A clear no, carried by an apology plus "it's difficult"
A scheduling question about next week
config.why: East Asian norms often avoid a direct "no" — the apology-plus-difficulty formula carries the refusal, which a literal-minded learner hears as a maybe. The American "we'll see", meanwhile, is often a no where a German hears a schedule.
